Central Asia / Steppe.0: The steppe and oases were home to hunter-gatherers and, increasingly, herders and farmers. Farming villages like Jeitun appeared in Turkmenistan c. 6000 BC, while the Botai people of northern Kazakhstan were herding, riding and milking horses by c. 3500 BC, a change that would transform steppe life for millennia.
Central Asia / Steppe.1: Yamnaya herders on the Pontic-Caspian steppe, living in wagons and burying leaders under kurgan mounds, spread far east and west, probably carrying Indo-European languages. Related Afanasievo herders reached the Altai, and in the southern oases the Oxus civilization (BMAC) built fortified towns with bronze metalwork c. 2300 BC.
Central Asia / Steppe.2: Around 2000 BC the Sintashta people of the southern Urals built fortified settlements and the first spoked-wheel chariots. The related Andronovo culture spread herding, bronze and horse warfare across the steppe, and Indo-Iranian speakers moved south toward Iran and India as the Oxus oasis towns declined.
Central Asia / Steppe.3: True mounted nomadism took hold as riders with bows and mobile herds replaced wagon-based life. Scythians, Saka and Cimmerians dominated the grasslands, burying chiefs in rich kurgans such as Arzhan in Tuva and creating gold animal-style art, while some raided deep into the Near East in the 600s BC.
Central Asia / Steppe.4: Persia's Achaemenid kings conquered the southern oases, turning Bactria, Sogdiana and Chorasmia into tribute-paying provinces. Cyrus the Great reportedly died fighting the nomadic Massagetae c. 530 BC, and beyond the Persian frontier Saka and Scythian horse peoples remained independent, trading and raiding across the grasslands.
Central Asia / Steppe.5: The Achaemenid satrapies of Bactria and Sogdiana supplied Persia with soldiers, lapis lazuli and gold. On the steppe, Scythians north of the Black Sea traded with Greek colonies and were described by Herodotus, while the Pazyryk people of the Altai left frozen tombs preserving tattooed bodies, carpets and horses.
Central Asia / Steppe.6: Alexander the Great fought a hard campaign in Bactria and Sogdiana in 329 to 327 BC, facing local resistance under Spitamenes and marrying the Bactrian noblewoman Roxana. After his death the Seleucids inherited the region, while on the western steppe the Sarmatians began displacing the Scythians.
Central Asia / Steppe.7: Greek settlers in Bactria broke from the Seleucids c. 250 BC to form the Greco-Bactrian kingdom, and the Parthians rose to the west. In Mongolia Modu Chanyu forged the Xiongnu confederation in 209 BC, crushing rivals like the Yuezhi and forcing the new Han dynasty to pay tribute.
Central Asia / Steppe.8: Driven west by the Xiongnu, the Yuezhi and Saka overran Greco-Bactria c. 130 BC. Han China fought back: Zhang Qian's missions of 138 to 126 BC mapped the western lands, Han armies pushed into the Tarim Basin and Ferghana for horses, and the trade routes later called the Silk Road began to take shape.
Central Asia / Steppe.9: The Xiongnu weakened and split, and one faction under Huhanye submitted to Han China in 51 BC. Han established a Protectorate of the Western Regions over the Tarim oasis cities c. 60 BC, while the Yuezhi settled in Bactria in five clans and Parthia controlled the routes to the west.
Central Asia / Steppe.10: One Yuezhi clan under Kujula Kadphises united the others c. AD 30 to found the Kushan Empire, which grew from Bactria into northern India. The Xiongnu split permanently in AD 48, and the Han general Ban Chao reasserted Chinese control over the Tarim oases, securing the Silk Road.
Central Asia / Steppe.11: The Kushan Empire peaked under Kanishka (c. 127 to 150), a patron of Buddhism whose lands linked Rome, Parthia, India and China. Buddhist monks and Sogdian merchants carried ideas and goods along the Silk Road, while the Xianbei replaced the Xiongnu as masters of the Mongolian steppe.
Central Asia / Steppe.12: Kushan power faded as Sasanian Persia seized its western lands c. 230s and set up Kushano-Sasanian rulers in Bactria. The Xianbei confederation fractured after its great leader's death, and Sogdian merchant families from Samarkand and Bukhara became the main middlemen of the Silk Road trade.
Central Asia / Steppe.13: Peoples from the eastern steppe pressed in every direction. The Huns appeared north of the Caspian and in the 370s crossed the Volga, defeating the Alans and Goths and setting off migrations into the Roman world. Chionites and Kidarites took Bactria, and Xianbei and other nomads ruled much of northern China.
Central Asia / Steppe.14: The Rouran Khaganate dominated Mongolia, while the Hephthalites, or White Huns, built an empire over Bactria and parts of the Tarim, defeating and killing the Sasanian king Peroz in 484. Far to the west, Attila's Huns terrorized Europe until his death in 453.
Central Asia / Steppe.15: In 552 the Turks under Bumin overthrew their Rouran overlords and founded the Göktürk Khaganate, the first empire to carry the Turkic name, stretching from Manchuria to the Black Sea. Allied with Persia they destroyed the Hephthalites c. 560, though the empire soon split into eastern and western halves.
Central Asia / Steppe.16: Tang China defeated the Eastern Turks in 630 and the Western Turks by 657, ruling the Tarim oases through protectorates. Meanwhile Arab armies conquered Persia and reached Khorasan by the 650s. The pilgrim Xuanzang crossed the region, and in 682 the Turks revived their khaganate in Mongolia.
Central Asia / Steppe.17: Arab armies under Qutayba conquered Bukhara and Samarkand in 705 to 715, and in 751 the Abbasids defeated Tang forces at Talas, helping Islam spread through Central Asia. The Turks carved the Orkhon inscriptions, then were overthrown in 744 by the Uyghurs, who rescued the Tang during the An Lushan Rebellion.
Central Asia / Steppe.18: The Kyrgyz destroyed the Uyghur Khaganate in 840, and Uyghurs resettled in the Turfan and Gansu oases, becoming farmers and traders. In Bukhara the Persian Samanid dynasty built a brilliant Islamic state, while the Khazars and Pechenegs dominated the western steppe north of the Caspian and Black Seas.
Central Asia / Steppe.19: Samanid Bukhara flourished as a center of Persian poetry and Islamic learning, but the Turkic Kara-Khanids, who converted to Islam c. 934, took Bukhara in 999. Turkic Ghaznavids rose in Afghanistan, the Khitan built the Liao empire to the east, and the Rus' destroyed the Khazar state in the 960s.
Central Asia / Steppe.20: Oghuz Turks led by the Seljuk family moved out of the Aral region, defeated the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan in 1040 and conquered Persia. The Kara-Khanids ruled the oases, Kipchak and Cuman nomads dominated the western steppe, and scholars like Ibn Sina and al-Biruni made the region a center of science.
Central Asia / Steppe.21: Khitan refugees founded the Qara Khitai state and crushed the Seljuks at Qatwan in 1141. Late in the century the Khwarezmian shahs built a large but brittle empire, while in Mongolia rival tribes such as the Tatars, Keraites, Naimans and Mongols fought each other. Temüjin was born c. 1162.
Central Asia / Steppe.22: In 1206 Temüjin united the Mongol tribes as Genghis Khan, then destroyed the Khwarezmian Empire in 1219 to 1221 with enormous slaughter. His successors built the largest land empire in history, which split after 1260 into the Golden Horde, Chagatai Khanate, Ilkhanate and Yuan, while trade flowed under the Pax Mongolica.
Central Asia / Steppe.23: The Golden Horde converted to Islam under Uzbeg Khan, the Chagatai Khanate broke apart, and plague probably spread along steppe routes. From 1370 to 1405 Timur, a Turkic-Mongol emir based in Samarkand, conquered Persia, crushed the Golden Horde and sacked Delhi and Damascus, building a short-lived empire.
Central Asia / Steppe.24: Timur's heirs presided over a cultural flowering, with Shah Rukh at Herat and the astronomer-prince Ulugh Beg building his observatory at Samarkand in the 1420s. The Golden Horde broke into rival khanates, the Oirats captured a Ming emperor in 1449, and the Kazakh Khanate emerged c. 1465.
Central Asia / Steppe.25: Shaybanid Uzbeks seized Samarkand in 1500, driving the Timurid Babur toward India, and founded the Khanate of Bukhara. Russia took Kazan in 1552 and Astrakhan in 1556 and began crossing into Siberia. As European sea routes grew, overland caravan trade became less central, and Tibetan Buddhism spread among Mongols.
Central Asia / Steppe.26: The Oirat Mongols formed the powerful Dzungar Khanate in western Mongolia and Xinjiang, while one Oirat group, the Kalmyks, migrated to the Volga. Russian traders and Cossacks swept across Siberia to the Pacific, and the Manchu Qing absorbed the southern Mongols and fought the Dzungar leader Galdan, defeating him in 1696.
Central Asia / Steppe.27: Dzungar attacks on the Kazakhs in 1723 began the 'Years of Great Disaster', and in 1731 the Kazakh Junior Horde sought Russian protection. Russia built fortress lines like Orenburg, while the khanates of Bukhara and Khiva weakened and were briefly overrun by the Persian conqueror Nader Shah in 1740.
Central Asia / Steppe.28: Exploiting a Dzungar succession crisis, the Qing conquered Dzungaria in 1755 to 1758, and war, smallpox and massacre nearly wiped out the Dzungar people. The Qing then took the Tarim oases, forming Xinjiang. The Kalmyks' 1771 flight from Russia ended in disaster, and Bukhara and Kokand gained new dynasties.
Central Asia / Steppe.29: Central Asia's oases were ruled by three Uzbek khanates, Bukhara, Khiva and the expanding Kokand, while the Qing held Xinjiang. Russia tightened its grip on the Kazakh steppe, abolishing the Middle Horde's khan in 1822, and Afghanistan's Durrani kingdom slid into civil war among rival princes.
Central Asia / Steppe.30: Britain and Russia began the 'Great Game' for influence. Britain invaded Afghanistan in 1839 but its army was destroyed retreating from Kabul in 1842, while a Russian winter march on Khiva failed. Kenesary Kasymov led a Kazakh revolt against Russia, and Bukhara executed two British officers in 1842.
Central Asia / Steppe.31: Russia conquered the heart of Central Asia, taking Tashkent in 1865, Samarkand in 1868 and Khiva in 1873, and made Bukhara a protectorate. The new province of Turkestan was turned toward cotton growing. In Xinjiang a great Muslim revolt allowed Yakub Beg to rule Kashgar from 1865.
Central Asia / Steppe.32: Russia annexed Kokand in 1876 and crushed the Turkmen at Geok Tepe in 1881, then built the Trans-Caspian Railway. Britain fought a second Afghan war in 1878 to 1880, and the Durand Line and Pamir agreements fixed Afghan borders. The Qing reconquered Xinjiang, making it a province in 1884.
Central Asia / Steppe.33: The Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 eased the Great Game by fixing spheres of influence. The Orenburg to Tashkent railway opened in 1906, tying the region to Russia, and Russian peasant settlers took Kazakh pastures. Muslim reformers called Jadids pushed for modern schools and new ideas.
Central Asia / Steppe.34: Mongolia broke from the collapsing Qing in 1911. In 1916 a revolt against Russian labor conscription was savagely crushed, sending many Kazakhs and Kyrgyz fleeing to China. After 1917 the Bolsheviks destroyed the Kokand autonomy and fought Basmachi rebels, and Afghanistan won full independence in 1919.
Central Asia / Steppe.35: The Soviets abolished the old khanates and in 1924 drew new national republics such as the Uzbek and Turkmen SSRs. Mongolia became the world's second communist state. Soviet campaigns attacked Islam and the veil, and in Afghanistan King Amanullah's rapid reforms provoked a revolt that toppled him in 1929.
Central Asia / Steppe.36: Stalin's collectivization forced Kazakh nomads onto collective farms, and the resulting famine of 1930 to 1933 killed about 1.5 million people, a huge share of the population. The purges of 1937 to 1938 destroyed local elites. In 1939 Soviet and Mongolian forces defeated Japan at Khalkhin Gol.
Central Asia / Steppe.37: During World War II whole factories and deported peoples, including Chechens, Volga Germans and Crimean Tatars, were sent to Central Asia. A Soviet-backed East Turkestan Republic existed in northern Xinjiang until the Chinese Communists took the region in 1949, the year the Soviets tested their first atomic bomb at Semipalatinsk.
Central Asia / Steppe.38: Khrushchev's Virgin Lands campaign ploughed up vast areas of the Kazakh steppe for wheat and brought in Slavic settlers. The Baikonur Cosmodrome opened, launching Sputnik in 1957. China created the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region in 1955 and sent Han settlers, while Afghanistan accepted Soviet aid.
Central Asia / Steppe.39: Soviet planners diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to grow cotton, and the Aral Sea began to shrink. Yuri Gagarin launched from Baikonur in 1961, Tashkent was rebuilt after a 1966 earthquake, and the Sino-Soviet split brought armed border clashes in 1969, including along Xinjiang.
Central Asia / Steppe.40: Under Brezhnev, Uzbekistan became a vast cotton monoculture run by entrenched local party bosses. In Afghanistan the monarchy fell in 1973, a communist coup followed in 1978, and in December 1979 the Soviet army invaded, beginning a war that would last ten years.
Central Asia / Steppe.41: The Soviet-Afghan War killed perhaps a million or more Afghans and drove millions into exile, while mujahideen received US, Pakistani and Saudi support. Soviet troops withdrew in 1989. Gorbachev's reforms exposed the Uzbek cotton scandal and the Aral disaster, and protests erupted in Almaty in 1986.
Central Asia / Steppe.42: When the USSR collapsed in 1991, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan became independent, mostly led by former Communist bosses. Tajikistan suffered a civil war from 1992 to 1997, Mongolia became a democracy, and in Afghanistan the Taliban seized Kabul in 1996 after years of civil war.
Central Asia / Steppe.43: After 9/11 the US invaded Afghanistan in 2001, toppling the Taliban and opening bases in Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. Oil and gas wealth transformed Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan, China and Russia formed the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and protests brought violence in Andijan and a revolution in Kyrgyzstan in 2005.
Central Asia / Steppe.44: China launched its Belt and Road Initiative in Kazakhstan in 2013, pouring money into railways and pipelines, and from c. 2017 detained large numbers of Uyghurs in Xinjiang camps. Uzbekistan opened up after Karimov's death in 2016, Nazarbayev stepped down in 2019, and NATO's Afghan combat mission ended in 2014.
Central Asia / Steppe.45: The US withdrew from Afghanistan in 2021 and the Taliban returned, sharply restricting women's lives. Kazakhstan saw deadly unrest in 2022, and Russia's invasion of Ukraine pushed the region to diversify trade and routes. Rivalry among Russia, China, Turkey and the West for influence intensified.

India.0: South Asia had been home to hunter-gatherers for tens of thousands of years, who left paintings at sites like Bhimbetka. At Mehrgarh, c. 7000 BC, people began farming wheat and barley and herding cattle, and by the 4000s BC farming villages had spread across the Indus plains.
India.1: The Indus Valley civilization flourished c. 2600 to 1900 BC in planned cities like Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira, with brick houses, drains and standard weights. Its people used a still-undeciphered script and traded with Mesopotamia, while farming villages spread elsewhere in the subcontinent.
India.2: The Indus cities declined c. 1900 BC as rivers shifted and the climate dried, and people moved into smaller villages. From c. 1500 BC Indo-Aryan speaking herders settled the Punjab, composing the Rigveda, and the Vedic age began, with cattle wealth, fire sacrifices and warrior chiefs.
India.3: Vedic peoples moved east into the Ganges plain, clearing forest with iron tools and growing rice. Kingdoms like the Kurus and Panchalas emerged, the varna social order hardened, and the early Upanishads explored ideas of soul and rebirth. By c. 600 BC sixteen large states had formed.
India.4: The sixteen states competed for power, and Magadha rose under King Bimbisara. Towns and coinage grew, and new teachers challenged Vedic ritual: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, and Mahavira of the Jains taught in Magadha. In c. 518 BC Persia's Darius took the Indus region as a province.
India.5: Magadha expanded under Ajatashatru, defeating the Vajji confederacy and Kosala and building a fort at Pataliputra that became its capital. Buddhist and Jain communities spread after their founders' deaths, and the grammarian Panini (c. 5th or 4th century BC) codified Sanskrit. Persia still ruled the northwest.
India.6: The Nanda kings made Magadha rich and feared. Alexander the Great reached the Indus in 326 BC and defeated King Porus, but his army refused to go farther. In 322 BC Chandragupta Maurya, advised by Chanakya, overthrew the Nandas and founded the Maurya Empire, later taking the northwest from Seleucus.
India.7: The Maurya Empire reached its peak under Ashoka. After his bloody Kalinga War c. 261 BC he embraced Buddhism and dhamma, carving edicts on rocks and pillars and sending missions to Sri Lanka and beyond. After his death c. 232 BC the empire weakened, while Tamil kingdoms ruled the far south.
India.8: The last Maurya was killed c. 185 BC by his general Pushyamitra, founder of the Shunga dynasty. Indo-Greek kings such as Menander ruled the northwest, the Satavahanas rose in the Deccan, and Buddhist sites like Sanchi and Bharhut were richly decorated. Saka nomads began arriving from Central Asia.
India.9: India was divided among many powers. Saka (Indo-Scythian) kings ruled the northwest, the Kanvas replaced the Shungas in Magadha, and the Satavahanas controlled the Deccan. In the Tamil south the Chera, Chola and Pandya kingdoms flourished, and sea trade with the Roman world began to grow.
India.10: Indo-Parthian kings such as Gondophares ruled the northwest, and Kushan rulers from Bactria expanded into northern India. Roman ships using the monsoon winds bought pepper, gems and textiles at ports like Muziris, paying in gold. Tamil Sangam poetry celebrated the kings and life of the south.
India.11: Under Kanishka the Kushans ruled from Peshawar and Mathura, sponsoring Buddhism as Mahayana ideas spread. Gandhara and Mathura artists made some of the first images of the Buddha. In the Deccan the Satavahanas revived, and around 150 the Saka ruler Rudradaman left an early long Sanskrit inscription.
India.12: The Kushan and Satavahana empires declined, and India broke into regional kingdoms. Sasanian Persia took the old Kushan northwest, Western Satraps ruled Gujarat, and the Vakatakas rose in the Deccan. Hindu traditions centered on Vishnu and Shiva developed further in texts like the Puranas.
India.13: In 320 Chandragupta I founded the Gupta Empire in the Ganges valley. His son Samudragupta won wide conquests, and Chandragupta II defeated the Western Satraps, controlling trade to the west. Gupta courts patronized Sanskrit literature, including the poet Kalidasa, and the Pallavas rose in the south.
India.14: The Gupta golden age continued, with Nalanda founded as a great center of learning and the Chinese pilgrim Faxian praising the realm. In 499 Aryabhata wrote on astronomy and place-value mathematics. In the late 400s Huna invaders from Central Asia attacked the northwest, straining Gupta power.
India.15: The Gupta Empire collapsed as Huna kings like Mihirakula ruled the northwest until they were pushed back c. 528. Northern India fragmented among regional dynasties, the Chalukyas rose at Badami in the Deccan, and the astronomer Varahamihira worked. In the Tamil south devotional bhakti poetry began to spread.
India.16: Harsha of Kanauj (606 to 647) united much of the north, and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang studied at Nalanda. The Chalukya king Pulakeshin II stopped Harsha in the Deccan and fought the Pallavas, who built the shore monuments at Mahabalipuram. Brahmagupta set out rules for zero in 628.
India.17: In 711 to 712 Arab forces under Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh, bringing Islam to the subcontinent. Three powers, the Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Buddhist Palas of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan, fought over Kanauj. The Kailasa temple at Ellora was carved, and Adi Shankara taught Advaita philosophy.
India.18: The three-way struggle for Kanauj continued, with the Pratiharas dominant in the north under Mihira Bhoja. The Palas supported Buddhist universities at Nalanda and Vikramashila, the Rashtrakutas were among the strongest Deccan powers, and the Chola dynasty revived c. 850 around Thanjavur in the Tamil south.
India.19: The Pratiharas declined after Rashtrakuta raids, and the north splintered into Rajput kingdoms such as the Chandelas, who later built Khajuraho. The Rashtrakutas fell in 973, and the Cholas grew powerful under Rajaraja I from 985. Late in the century Turkic Ghaznavid raiders appeared in the northwest.
India.20: Mahmud of Ghazni raided northern India repeatedly from 1000 to 1027, looting temples like Somnath, and the Ghaznavids annexed the Punjab. In the south the Chola Empire peaked: Rajaraja built the great temple at Thanjavur and Rajendra I's navy raided Srivijaya in 1025. Al-Biruni wrote a famous study of India.
India.21: Rajput kingdoms, among them Prithviraj Chauhan's, dominated the north while the Cholas slowly weakened. Muhammad of Ghor invaded, losing at Tarain in 1191 but winning in 1192 and taking Delhi. Turkic forces swept into Bengal, and Nalanda was sacked c. 1193, a heavy blow to Buddhism in India.
India.22: In 1206 the Turkic general Qutb ud-Din Aibak founded the Delhi Sultanate, building the Qutb Minar. Sultans like Iltutmish, Razia, India's first Muslim woman ruler, and Balban held off Mongol raids, while Persian became the court language. The south was ruled by Pandyas, Hoysalas and Kakatiyas.
India.23: Alauddin Khalji repelled the Mongols and raided the far south, and Muhammad bin Tughluq experimented with token coins and moving his capital. Southern rebels founded the Vijayanagara Empire in 1336 and the Bahmani Sultanate in 1347. In 1398 Timur sacked Delhi, shattering the sultanate's power.
India.24: After Timur, Delhi's Sayyid and Lodi sultans ruled a shrunken realm, while Bengal, Gujarat and Malwa became independent sultanates. Vijayanagara grew rich in the south, and the Bahmani state split into Deccan sultanates. Kabir and Guru Nanak preached devotion beyond caste, and in 1498 Vasco da Gama reached Calicut.
India.25: The Portuguese seized Goa in 1510. In 1526 Babur, a Timurid prince from Central Asia, won at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire. Akbar the Great (1556 to 1605) conquered most of the north, built an efficient administration and practiced religious tolerance, while Vijayanagara fell in 1565.
India.26: The Mughals were at their richest under Jahangir and Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal, and largest under Aurangzeb. European trading companies set up posts, with the English East India Company founded in 1600. Indian cotton textiles were in demand worldwide, and Shivaji founded the Maratha kingdom in 1674.
India.27: After Aurangzeb died in 1707, Mughal power crumbled as governors in Hyderabad, Bengal and Awadh became virtually independent. The Marathas expanded across central India under their Peshwas, and in 1739 the Persian ruler Nader Shah sacked Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne. British-French rivalry grew.
India.28: The East India Company's victory at Plassey in 1757 gave it Bengal, and by 1765 it collected the province's taxes. The Afghans defeated the Marathas at Panipat in 1761, a famine devastated Bengal in 1770, and the Company fought Mysore, killing Tipu Sultan in 1799.
India.29: The British defeated the Marathas in 1803 to 1818, making the Company the dominant power in India while many princes ruled under its protection. Ranjit Singh built a strong Sikh kingdom in the Punjab. Missionaries were allowed in from 1813, and reformers like Ram Mohan Roy debated Hindu custom.
India.30: Company rule brought reforms and intrusions: sati was banned in 1829 and English-language education promoted from 1835. British machine-made cloth undercut Indian weavers. After Ranjit Singh's death, the British fought two wars with the Sikhs and annexed the Punjab in 1849, and launched a disastrous war in Afghanistan.
India.31: Railways and telegraphs spread from 1853, while annexations of princely states fed resentment. The great Indian Rebellion of 1857 was crushed with heavy reprisals, and in 1858 the British Crown replaced the Company, beginning the British Raj. Universities opened, and a cotton boom followed the American Civil War.
India.32: Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India in 1877 even as the Great Famine of 1876 to 1878 killed millions. Educated Indians founded the Indian National Congress in 1885, while reform movements like the Arya Samaj and Sayyid Ahmad Khan's Aligarh college reshaped Hindu and Muslim life.
India.33: Viceroy Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905, sparking the Swadeshi movement to boycott British goods. The Muslim League was founded in 1906, Congress split between moderates and radicals like Tilak, and the 1909 reforms gave Indians limited seats with separate Muslim electorates.
India.34: The capital moved to Delhi in 1911 and over a million Indians served in World War I. Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and began peaceful protests. In 1919 British troops killed hundreds at Amritsar, while the influenza pandemic killed millions, turning many against British rule.
India.35: Gandhi led the mass Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920 to 1922, joined with Muslim Khilafat activists, before calling it off after violence. Protests met the all-white Simon Commission in 1928, revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh emerged, and in 1929 Congress demanded full independence.
India.36: Gandhi's Salt March in 1930 launched civil disobedience, and talks in London followed. The 1935 Government of India Act widened self-rule, and Congress won provincial elections in 1937, while Jinnah's Muslim League grew. In 1939 Britain declared war for India without consulting Indian leaders.
India.37: The Muslim League called for Pakistan in 1940, Congress launched Quit India in 1942, and the Bengal famine of 1943 killed about 3 million. In 1947 India gained independence and was partitioned into India and Pakistan amid mass migration and killing. Gandhi was assassinated in 1948.
India.38: India became a republic under its new constitution in 1950, and its first general election in 1951 to 1952 was the largest democratic vote ever held. Prime Minister Nehru pursued state-led industry, non-alignment and secular democracy, and states were redrawn along language lines in 1956. Pakistan saw its first coup in 1958.
India.39: India took Goa from Portugal in 1961 but lost a border war with China in 1962. Nehru died in 1964, India and Pakistan fought in 1965, and Indira Gandhi became prime minister in 1966. New high-yield seeds launched the Green Revolution, ending fears of mass famine.
India.40: In 1971 India intervened in East Pakistan's war of independence, defeating Pakistan and helping create Bangladesh. India tested a nuclear device in 1974. Indira Gandhi's Emergency of 1975 to 1977 suspended civil liberties, and voters ousted her in 1977, though she returned in 1980.
India.41: Indira Gandhi ordered troops into the Golden Temple in 1984 and was assassinated by her Sikh bodyguards, followed by anti-Sikh massacres. The Bhopal gas leak killed thousands that year. Her son Rajiv promoted technology, and an insurgency broke out in Kashmir in 1989.
India.42: Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated in 1991, and that year's economic crisis led to liberalization that opened India to trade and investment. The Babri Masjid's destruction in 1992 brought deadly riots and the rise of Hindu nationalist politics. India and Pakistan both tested nuclear weapons in 1998.
India.43: India's economy grew rapidly, driven by IT services and outsourcing, and a new middle class expanded. Deadly riots struck Gujarat in 2002, the Indian Ocean tsunami hit in 2004, and Manmohan Singh led a Congress coalition. The 2008 Mumbai terror attacks killed 166 people.
India.44: Cheap smartphones and data connected hundreds of millions of Indians. Narendra Modi's BJP won a majority in 2014, introducing a national biometric ID, demonetization in 2016 and a national sales tax. In 2019 the government ended Kashmir's special status and a citizenship law sparked mass protests.
India.45: Covid-19 brought a harsh lockdown in 2020 and a deadly wave in 2021, and Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Himalayas. In 2023 India became the world's most populous country and Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole. Modi won a third term in 2024.

China.0: Early humans lived in China for hundreds of thousands of years. From c. 7000 BC people farmed rice along the Yangtze and millet along the Yellow River, building Neolithic villages. Cultures such as Yangshao, with painted pottery, Hemudu and Hongshan, with carved jades, flourished by c. 5000 to 3000 BC.
China.1: Neolithic societies grew more complex, with walled towns, elite burials and fine jades. The Liangzhu culture near the Yangtze built large water works, and the Longshan culture made thin black pottery. Later Chinese tradition placed the legendary Yellow Emperor and Xia dynasty in this age, and bronze-working appeared at its end.
China.2: The Erlitou culture, possibly the Xia, built palaces c. 1900 BC. The Shang dynasty (c. 1600 to 1046 BC) ruled the Yellow River plain with bronze vessels, chariots, human sacrifice and oracle-bone writing, the ancestor of Chinese script. In 1046 BC the Zhou conquered the Shang, claiming the Mandate of Heaven.
China.3: Zhou kings granted lands to relatives and allies who ruled them as lords. In 771 BC invaders sacked the western capital, and the court moved east to Luoyang, beginning the Spring and Autumn period. The kings lost real power as states like Qi and Jin led coalitions, and iron began to appear.
China.4: The Zhou kings were figureheads while states like Jin, Chu, Qi, Wu and Yue fought for supremacy. Amid the turmoil Confucius (551 to 479 BC) taught that good government came from virtue and ritual, and tradition credits Laozi with founding Daoism. Iron tools and written law codes spread.
China.5: The Warring States period began c. 475 BC, and the great state of Jin split into Han, Zhao and Wei. Rulers built large infantry armies with crossbows and centralized bureaucracies. The 'Hundred Schools of Thought' flourished, including Mozi's ideas of universal love.
China.6: War grew larger and more ruthless. Shang Yang's Legalist reforms from 356 BC made Qin a disciplined military state, Zhao adopted nomad-style cavalry, and states built walls against rivals and steppe raiders. Thinkers such as Mencius and Zhuangzi debated human nature and the good life.
China.7: Qin conquered its rivals, and in 221 BC its king became Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. He standardized script, coins and weights, linked walls into a Great Wall and was buried with the Terracotta Army. Harsh rule sparked revolts after his death, and Liu Bang founded the Han dynasty in 206 to 202 BC.
China.8: The Han consolidated imperial rule after crushing a rebellion of princes in 154 BC. Emperor Wu (141 to 87 BC) made Confucianism the state ideology, set up salt and iron monopolies, fought the Xiongnu and expanded into Korea, Vietnam and Central Asia as the Silk Road opened. Sima Qian wrote his great history.
China.9: Han China was at its height, with a large bureaucracy and growing trade. The Xiongnu submitted in 51 BC, and a protectorate oversaw the western oases. But wealthy landed families grew powerful and court politics fell under the influence of empresses' clans, paving the way for the usurper Wang Mang.
China.10: A census in AD 2 counted nearly 60 million people. Wang Mang seized the throne in AD 9 and attempted radical reforms, but floods and the Red Eyebrows revolt destroyed him. The Han was restored in 25 with its capital at Luoyang, Buddhism arrived from Central Asia, and Ban Chao secured the Tarim Basin.
China.11: The Eastern Han produced inventions like improved paper, traditionally credited to Cai Lun in 105, and Zhang Heng's seismoscope. But eunuchs and consort clans fought over a weak court, landlords grew stronger, and the Yellow Turban Rebellion of 184 opened the way for warlords to tear the empire apart.
China.12: The Han dynasty ended in 220, and China split into the Three Kingdoms of Wei, Shu and Wu, an age later romanticized in literature. Decades of war cut the registered population sharply. In 280 the Jin dynasty briefly reunified China, and Buddhism continued to spread.
China.13: Civil war among Jin princes opened the north to non-Chinese peoples such as the Xiongnu and Xianbei, who sacked Luoyang in 311. The north fractured into the Sixteen Kingdoms, while the Eastern Jin ruled the south from Jiankang (Nanjing) and many northerners fled south. Buddhism grew strongly.
China.14: The Xianbei-led Northern Wei united north China in 439, carved Buddhist cave temples at Yungang, and adopted Chinese ways under Emperor Xiaowen, who moved the capital to Luoyang. In the south a series of short-lived dynasties ruled. This era is called the Northern and Southern Dynasties.
China.15: Northern Wei split in 534, and the south's Liang dynasty became a great patron of Buddhism before civil war wrecked it. In 581 Yang Jian founded the Sui dynasty, and in 589 he conquered the south, reunifying China after nearly three centuries of division.
China.16: The Sui built the Grand Canal (605 to 611) linking north and south but collapsed after costly wars in Korea. The Tang dynasty, founded in 618, made Chang'an a cosmopolitan capital, defeated the Turks and expanded into Central Asia. Wu Zetian ruled as China's only empress regnant from 690 to 705.
China.17: Under Emperor Xuanzong the Tang reached a cultural high point, with poets like Li Bai and Du Fu. Defeat at Talas in 751 and the An Lushan Rebellion of 755 to 763 devastated the empire, and afterward regional military governors grew powerful while the court survived in a weaker form.
China.18: The late Tang struggled with eunuch power and regional governors. In 845 the court persecuted Buddhism, closing thousands of monasteries. The Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated printed book, and the Huang Chao Rebellion of 874 to 884 sacked major cities and ruined the dynasty.
China.19: The Tang fell in 907, and China split into the Five Dynasties in the north and Ten Kingdoms in the south. The Khitan Liao empire took lands near Beijing. In 960 the general Zhao Kuangyin founded the Song dynasty, which reunified most of China and placed civilian officials above generals.
China.20: The Song saw an economic revolution: paper money, movable type, the magnetic compass and gunpowder weapons all appeared, rice farming expanded and cities boomed as population passed about 100 million. But the Song paid tribute to the Liao and Tangut Xi Xia, and Wang Anshi's reforms divided the court.
China.21: The Jurchen Jin destroyed the Liao and captured the Song capital Kaifeng in 1127. The Song survived in the south as the Southern Song, based at Hangzhou, prospering through trade and sea commerce. Zhu Xi shaped Neo-Confucianism, which would guide Chinese thought for centuries.
China.22: The Mongols destroyed Xi Xia, conquered the Jin in 1234 and finally the Southern Song in 1279. Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271 with his capital at Dadu, today's Beijing. Mongols and Central Asians held top posts, while visitors like Marco Polo described the empire's wealth.
China.23: Yuan rule weakened amid epidemics, Yellow River floods and inflation, and the Red Turban rebellions began in 1351. Zhu Yuanzhang, a former peasant and monk, drove out the Mongols in 1368 and founded the Ming dynasty, ruling as an autocrat from Nanjing and rebuilding farming.
China.24: The Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Beijing and built the Forbidden City by 1420, and Zheng He led great fleets as far as East Africa from 1405 to 1433. After the Mongols captured an emperor in 1449, the Ming turned defensive, rebuilding the Great Wall and restricting overseas trade.
China.25: Ming China grew rich as American silver flowed in through Manila after 1571 and New World crops spread. Zhang Juzheng's reforms let taxes be paid in silver, the Portuguese settled Macau, and Jesuits like Matteo Ricci arrived. The Ming rebuilt the Great Wall in brick and aided Korea against Japan.
China.26: Famine, revolt and a weak court brought down the Ming when rebels took Beijing in 1644. The Manchus then seized the capital and founded the Qing dynasty, forcing men to wear the queue. The Kangxi Emperor crushed rebellions, took Taiwan in 1683 and fixed the Russian border in 1689.
China.27: Under the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors the Qing were at peace and prosperous, and the population grew rapidly. Yongzheng reformed taxes and created the Grand Council, the Qing extended control over Tibet, and Europeans bought ever more tea and porcelain. Christianity was banned in 1724.
China.28: Qianlong conquered Dzungaria and the Tarim oases, doubling Qing territory. Foreign trade was confined to Canton from 1757, and Britain's Macartney mission of 1793 failed to win better terms. As the population neared 300 million, corruption spread and the White Lotus Rebellion broke out in 1796.
China.29: The Jiaqing Emperor suppressed the White Lotus rebels and executed the corrupt minister Heshen, but the state was strained. British merchants smuggled growing amounts of opium from India, reversing the flow of silver. Population pressure caused land shortages and environmental damage.
China.30: Opium imports soared. When commissioner Lin Zexu destroyed British opium in 1839, Britain launched the First Opium War. The 1842 Treaty of Nanjing opened five ports, ceded Hong Kong and began the 'unequal treaties' that gave foreigners special rights in China.
China.31: The Taiping Rebellion, led by a man claiming to be Jesus's brother, killed 20 to 30 million people. Britain and France won the Second Opium War, burning the Summer Palace in 1860, and Russia took the Amur lands. Empress Dowager Cixi took power, and officials began 'self-strengthening' reforms.
China.32: Cixi dominated the court as famine in north China killed millions in 1876 to 1879. China lost influence over Vietnam to France, then lost Korea and Taiwan to Japan in 1894 to 1895. Foreign powers grabbed ports in 1898, and Cixi crushed the emperor's Hundred Days' Reform.
China.33: The anti-foreign Boxer Rebellion of 1900 to 1901 was crushed by eight foreign powers, which imposed a huge indemnity. Russia and Japan fought a war on Chinese soil, the Qing abolished the ancient civil service exams in 1905, and Sun Yat-sen's revolutionaries organized. Cixi died in 1908.
China.34: The 1911 revolution ended over 2,000 years of imperial rule, and the Republic of China was founded in 1912. Yuan Shikai's attempt to become emperor failed, and warlords divided the country after his death. When Japan gained German rights in Shandong, students protested on May Fourth, 1919.
China.35: The Chinese Communist Party was founded in 1921 and joined the Nationalists to fight the warlords. In 1927 Chiang Kai-shek turned on the Communists in Shanghai, beginning civil war, and set up a Nationalist government at Nanjing. Mao Zedong organized peasants in the countryside.
China.36: Japan seized Manchuria in 1931. Chiang's forces drove the Communists on the Long March of 1934 to 1935 to Yan'an. In 1937 Japan launched full-scale invasion, committing the Nanjing Massacre, and the Nationalist government retreated to Chongqing while the Communists waged guerrilla war.
China.37: China fought Japan until 1945 at a cost of many millions of lives, including the 1942 Henan famine. Civil war resumed in 1946, and the Communists won. On 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China, and Chiang's Nationalists fled to Taiwan.
China.38: China fought the US in the Korean War, carried out violent land reform and industrialized on the Soviet model. It took control of Tibet. After the brief Hundred Flowers openness came the Anti-Rightist purge, and Mao's Great Leap Forward from 1958 caused a famine that killed tens of millions.
China.39: China recovered slowly from the famine and broke with the Soviet Union, testing its own atomic bomb in 1964. In 1966 Mao launched the Cultural Revolution: Red Guards persecuted teachers, officials and 'class enemies', schools closed and millions were sent to the countryside.
China.40: China took the UN seat in 1971 and welcomed Nixon in 1972. In 1976 the Tangshan earthquake killed hundreds of thousands, Mao died, and the radical Gang of Four was arrested. From 1978 Deng Xiaoping launched market reforms, letting farmers sell their own crops and opening to the world.
China.41: The one-child policy began in 1980. Special economic zones like Shenzhen drew foreign investment, rural enterprises boomed and living standards rose rapidly, but inflation and corruption bred discontent. In 1989 the army crushed pro-democracy protests in Tiananmen Square.
China.42: Deng's 1992 southern tour relaunched market reforms, and coastal cities like Shanghai boomed while state firms laid off millions. Work began on the Three Gorges Dam. Britain returned Hong Kong in 1997 and Portugal returned Macau in 1999, while Taiwan held its first direct presidential election in 1996.
China.43: China joined the WTO in 2001 and became the 'workshop of the world', drawing hundreds of millions to factory cities. It sent its first astronaut into space in 2003 and hosted the Beijing Olympics in 2008, the same year an earthquake struck Sichuan and unrest flared in Tibet.
China.44: In 2010 China became the world's second-largest economy. Xi Jinping took power in 2012, launching an anti-corruption drive, the Belt and Road Initiative and island-building in the South China Sea. Controls tightened, with mass detentions in Xinjiang and, in 2019, huge protests in Hong Kong.
China.45: Covid-19 emerged in Wuhan, and China imposed strict 'zero-Covid' controls until late 2022. A 2020 security law curbed dissent in Hong Kong, and Xi won a third term in 2022. The population began to fall, a property slump slowed growth, and China led the world in electric vehicles and solar power.
